We commonly criticize Hollywood action fare for being dumb but the far far more infuriating thing to me about this (and about a lot of Nolan movies tbh) is how hard it tries to have the superficial appearance of being a smart movie that is about something. Early on in the film a copycat Batman asks the real one “what makes you different from me?” and the Joker is introduced as an ideological foil to Batman, as another character willing to use extrajudicial means to advance a personal agenda. The copycat Batman asks a good question! And the rest of the movie circles around it, seemingly exploring themes of vigilantism, legitimacy, force, or community- I say seemingly because it sets up that these might be interesting avenues to use the character of Batman to explore…. and then doesn’t. By the end, the only real justification of Batman offered by THE DARK KNIGHT is that he’s a rich guy with military hardware and that nobody can stop him. The movie spends so much effort asking the question and being self reflexive that I can’t help but be bothered by this “lesson.” The movie itself is expanding on the core idea of BEGINS- “what if Batman existed in the real world?” by asking a new question: “Isn’t the idea of Batman kind of stupid?”

Any moment the Joker isn't on screen, it's boring. I'm only giving it these 2 stars for the hospital explosion and Heath Ledger's performance, which is too good to be in this 154-minute-long disgrace to cinema. It's like a Michael Mann movie without any sauce. I think the main issue is while Mann's movies show such reverence and interest in its characters, Nolan could care less about fleshing his characters out beyond the first dimension so he can fit in more explosions and car chases. But don't worry, characters say Reddit philosophy quotes every other sentence so this movie is actually really deep and thought-provoking. Back to the characters, I find this to be the movie's biggest shortcoming. While Heath Ledger gives a fantastic performance as the Joker, the script he's working with offers him little help. Nolan's depiction of the Joker is so bland - he's an agent of chaos who does crime because he finds it fun. That's it. We never learn a thing about the Joker outside of his relationship to Batman. And that type of character can work. Anton Chigurh is a fantastic villain who fits a similar archetype to the Joker. But Chigurh works because we see the impact he has on the other characters in No Country for Old Men - how his nihilistic lack of motivation chills Ed to his core and makes him question everything he's been led to believe. But Batman/Bruce Wayne has no real character arc in this movie. In the first act his a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys, and in the third act he's still a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys. He learns nothing. He never grows. He never reflects on what the Joker represents, just chases him over and over until he finally catches him with the help of his cool gadgets. So what's the moral here? Batman just needed more gadgets to beat the Joker? The other characters in this film are of little interest either. Harvey Dent is a white knight ruthless prosecutor who chases down the bad guys and beats them up. Then he gets blown up and his world gets turned upside down because he chases down the people who wronged him and shoots them. I feel like this could be an interesting commentary on the criminal justice system being the other side of the coin of criminality itself, but the film is so afraid of depicting law enforcement with a shred of scrutiny that it plays it all completely straight. Harvey Dent is not a depiction of the corruption inherent in law enforcement, he's an awesome, flawless hero to all who is tragically brought down by the Joker. Because corruption isn't inherent in the system, rather it's propagated by a few bad apples like the Joker and his goons. How can I say this all so definitively? Because the movie tells us it definitively. It leaves nothing up to interpretation and tells us exactly what we should take away from each scene. "You either die a hero or live long enough to become the villain," "Some men just want to watch the world burn," etc. When characters aren't directly talking about what's happening in the scene or beating each other up, they're telling the audience what they should take away from the scene. Nolan's writing is so unsubtle I'm surprised he doesn't have Joker hold up a sign that says "I'm the bad guy." I genuinely have no idea why this film is so beloved. Maybe because it was such a shock in 2008 to see a superhero movie that's actually dark. But if you ignore the superhero dressing and analyze this film for what it is - a crime film - it just doesn't do anything to stand out among the plethora of far better crime films that have come before and since.

Looking back on this almost 20 years later and my biggest takeaway is how insecure this movie is. Dark Knight is CONSTANTLY SCREAMING its themes at you in the most dramatic, self indulgent way possible. You’ll have the Joker literally look at the screen and state “I’m an agent of chaos” while Gordon and Batman wax poetically on whether people are naturally good or evil. Worst of all, the movie will go out of its way to tell the viewer that some people are simply irredeemable and need to be put down. Contrast that to how the Spider-Man movies will try to tackle the heavy subject of villain redemption. Sure the execution is childish but at least it tries!   I came away with the theory that Nolan thought that superhero movies were not good enough to stand on their own so he had to water this down into the most grounded, serious, “adult” version of the Batman possible. The problem isn’t that The Dark Knight has nothing to say. It’s that it has so much confidence in how profound those things are that it rarely bothers to dramatize them. The movie is a long, slow, plodding mess that does not get the buy in necessary to take it self so seriously. Two hours and thirty minutes and no one gets developed. Gordon is always right and never pushed to grow, Harvey’s turn felt superficial and rudimentary, Rachel was literally in the movie to die. Worst of all, the Joker. We get so much time to develop and build on them relationship between him and Batman; how they’re mirrors of each other, how their philosophies are contradictory, how they mess with each other’s head. Instead we get Joker stating funny quips and theorize on le society. And I’m sorry but this movie and this performance is no where near good enough to justify the worship the Joker and this movie at large gets.

Para mí, The Dark Knight es la mejor película de la trilogía. Lo que más me gustó fue la forma en que se desarrolla el personaje de The Joker y cómo se opone ante Batman para intentar destruir Gotham. La historia es más compleja y madura que la de la primera película, y se nota que Nolan elevó el nivel en todos los aspectos. La actuación de Heath Ledger como Joker me pareció excelente. Consigue transmitir perfectamente la locura y el caos del personaje, convirtiéndolo en uno de los villanos más memorables del cine. Aunque hay momentos en los que la película puede sentirse un poco lenta o pesada, especialmente por su duración, sigue siendo una experiencia que vale la pena. Al terminarla me dejó una muy buena sensación y entendí por qué tanta gente la considera una de las mejores películas de superhéroes de todos los tiempos. Algo que hace especial a esta película es la forma en que Christopher Nolan utilizó cámaras IMAX para muchas de las escenas más importantes. Esto permitió mostrar Gotham, las persecuciones y las secuencias de acción con una escala impresionante que todavía hoy se siente espectacular. Además, Nolan intentó evitar el uso excesivo de CGI, prefiriendo efectos prácticos siempre que fuera posible. Gracias a esto, muchas escenas conservan una sensación de realismo que las hace envejecer mejor que otras películas de superhéroes de la misma época. Esa combinación entre IMAX, efectos prácticos y una dirección muy cuidada es una de las razones por las que la trilogía sigue siendo tan recordada.

This is everyone’s favorite adaptation of Batman? Are we watching the same movie? In celebration of the Lego Batman’s dlc release tomorrow I decided that this movie needed a rewatch. First, Heath Ledger is phenomenal. Outside of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash , Heath Ledger is probably my favorite performance ever. Bale has never completely convinced me as either Bruce Wayne or Batman. And the voice sucks!!!! Pattinson’s Bruce feels like someone consumed by being Batman while Bale’s Bruce often feels like he is simply operating within Nolan’s crime story. I heavily prefer Reeves’ dark and gothic Gotham to Nolan’s much brighter Chicago setting city. There are times when TDK feels less like a Batman movie and more like an extremely well-made crime thriller that happens to have Batman in it. How can I even call this a Batman movie when Joker commands most of the screen time? Batman feels strangely disconnected from being the “world’s greatest detective”. The fingerprint reconstruction scene is supposed to demonstrate his detective abilities, but it mostly amounts to technology doing the detective work for him rather than Batman being this great detective with supreme intelligence. The same goes for his equipment. Reeves makes Bruce’s obsessive commitment to building and modifying his own gear part of his characterization whereas Nolan’s Batman has Lucius Fox seemingly hand him whatever the plot requires. And what exactly is this sorry ass excuse for this brightly lit Batcave? Some of the movie’s logic also loses me. The entire Hong Kong sequence feels excessive and out of place. Batman supposedly doesn’t kill despite blowing things up everywhere he goes. Rachel falls off a skyscraper and walks away seemingly unharmed. More importantly, the Joker’s plans work with almost supernatural precision. Every person seems to react exactly as he anticipates, every piece falls into place, and almost nothing meaningfully disrupts his schemes. Ledger is so magnetic that he makes you want to overlook it but it’s hard. I also understand the thematic purpose of the Joker having no conventional motive. He represents chaos and wants to prove that civilized people can be pushed into abandoning their morals. But committing chaos for the sake of it has never been as interesting to me as it apparently is to everyone else. The character motivation feels deliberately vague in a way that doesn’t completely work for me. Still, I don’t want my complaints to make it sound like I think this is a bad movie. Far from it. Nolan knows how to construct a great movie, and there are some incredible sequences here. The truck flip and the hospital blowing up remain ridiculously cool. I also wonder how much of the Batman debate is generational. A lot of millennials grew up with Bale as the Batman, while Gen Z got Pattinson at a formative age. Maybe I’m simply more drawn to what Reeves thinks Batman should be: this lonely gothic loser detective boy that’s inseparable from Gotham itself. I just think Reeves’ The Batman runs laps around this iteration of Batman. The Dark Knight is a good movie but I’m just not convinced it’s my version of a great Batman movie. B+ish

It’s really interesting how for a movie all marketed and focusing around the Joker and the pandaemonium he causes, how the central ideas all revolve around duality. At it’s core it’s all about honing in on characters wants vs their needs. Selfish desires vs responsibilities. Batman desperately wants Rachel, to settle down and have a happy life. But is obviously responsible to keeping up his mantle as Batman. By letting Harvey be Gothams white night Batman in his hopes and dreams is no longer needed. But unlike Bruce, Harvey can be Gotham’s savior and Rachel. Or so he thinks. Harvey thinks he can have his cake and eat it too. Using the law to put all the cities criminals behind bars, but attempting to do so under an inherently corrupt and decaying system makes him vulnerable to the same dangers that Batman himself is. You can do this with every character and it just keeps looping around like a snake eating its own tail. While understanding want vs need is such a basic attribute to solid screenplays and character work, this film has that idea built into its thematic DNA. As a result it’s rock solid and still as absolutely perfect as it’s hyped up to be.
